claims.text: As-received 316L stainless steel has a typical austenitic microstructure.
As-received 316L stainless steel has no pronounced local chemical order.
Aging at 500–600 °C for 10–20 hours in an inert atmosphere will promote local chemical order in 316L stainless steel.
The aging treatment will not alter the overall alloy composition.
Aging-induced local chemical order in 316L will appear as nanoscale clusters enriched in Cr and minor alloying elements within the austenitic matrix.
Local chemical order lowers the mobility of corrosive species.
Ordered Cr-rich nanoclusters accelerate formation and stabilization of a continuous chromium-rich passive oxide film.
A continuous chromium-rich passive film hinders defect propagation and reduces corrosion attack.
Aged 316L specimens will have a significantly lower corrosion rate than as-received specimens.
Aged 316L specimens will have lower pit density than as-received specimens.
Aged 316L specimens will exhibit improved electrochemical impedance and a more uniform passive-film morphology.
The proposed mechanism applies to 316L under chemical-processing saline or acidic environments and pressurized-water nuclear-reactor coolant conditions.
Prior findings in high- and medium-entropy alloys support a role for local chemical order in passivation.
Direct evidence for local chemical order in conventional 316L and for its quantitative effect on corrosion remains uncertain.
A lack of statistically significant improvement in corrosion rate, pit density, or passive-film uniformity after aging would falsify the proposed LCO mechanism.
